facts.fact: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Mauryan Empire in 322 BCE.
Chandragupta overthrew the last Nanda ruler Dhanananda with Chanakya’s help.
Buddhist tradition makes the Mauryas a Kshatriya clan of the Gorakhpur region.
Brahmanical tradition says Chandragupta was born of a shudra woman at the Nanda court.
Chandragupta defeated Seleucus I in 305 BCE.
Chandragupta won Afghanistan, Baluchistan and the lands west of the Indus from Seleucus in return for 500 elephants.
Chandragupta’s empire included Bihar, Orissa and Bengal with the north and north-west.
Kerala, Tamil Nadu and parts of the North-East were outside Mauryan rule.
Chandragupta was an autocrat who kept all powers in his hands.
Pliny says Chandragupta had 600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry and 9,000 elephants.
Political unity was achieved for the first time in Indian history under the Mauryas.
Republican and oligarchic government ended and monarchy reached its height under the Mauryas.
The Mauryan capital was Pataliputra (present-day Patna).
The Mauryan Empire belongs to the Iron Age.
Chanakya was also known as Kautilya and Vishnugupta.
The Arthashastra was written by Kautilya in Sanskrit.
The Arthashastra has 15 books and 180 chapters.
The Arthashastra’s chapters fall into 3 broad divisions.
The Arthashastra stresses the king’s duty of Yogakshema (welfare) of the people.
The Arthashastra was compiled centuries after the Mauryas yet holds authentic information on their administration.
The Arthashastra is the most important source on the Mauryas.
Kautilya continued as prime minister under Bindusara.
The Arthashastra’s Saptanga theory gives the state seven limbs.
The Arthashastra notes the employment of slaves in agricultural operations on state farms.
R. Shamasastry found the Arthashastra in 1905 and published it in 1909.
Megasthenes was the ambassador of Seleucus at Chandragupta’s court.
Megasthenes wrote the Indica.
The Indica survives only in fragments collected by later Greek writers.
Mudrarakshasa was written by Vishakhadatta.
Mudrarakshasa belongs to the Gupta era but describes Chandragupta’s victory over the Nandas.
Buddhist literature and the Puranas also give accounts of the Mauryas.
Megasthenes divided Indian society into seven castes.
Megasthenes wrote that there was no slavery in India, which the Arthashastra contradicts.
Megasthenes calls district officers Agoranomoi and city officers Astynomoi.
Bindusara took the throne in 297 BCE.
The Greeks called Bindusara Amitragata (Amitrochates), meaning slayer of enemies.
Bindusara was also called Allitrochates by the Greeks.
Bindusara brought sixteen states of the peninsula under the empire.
Kalinga was the only peninsular kingdom outside Bindusara’s control.
Antiochus I sent the envoy Deimachus to Bindusara’s court.
Ptolemy II of Egypt sent the envoy Dionysius to the Mauryan court.
Bindusara followed the Ajivika sect.
Bindusara asked Antiochus I for sweet wine, dried figs and a sophist.
Bindusara sent Ashoka to quell the revolt of the people of Taxila.
Bindusara’s reign was important for continued links with the Greeks.
Ashoka ascended the throne around 268 BCE.
Ashoka was the son of Bindusara and grandson of Chandragupta.
Ashoka served as viceroy at Ujjain before his accession.
Ashoka was drawn to Buddhism by the monk Upagupta.
Ashoka was the first ruler to speak directly to his people through inscriptions.
Ashoka’s inscriptions number 39 in five classes.
The name Ashoka appears in the Maski edict.
Ashoka’s name occurs in copies of Minor Rock Edict I at three places in Karnataka and one in Madhya Pradesh.
Gujarra in Madhya Pradesh is one of the edicts that names Ashoka.
Most inscriptions call Ashoka Devanampiya Piyadasi.
Ashokan pillars were made at Chunar near Varanasi.
Ashokan inscriptions are found in India, Nepal, Pakistan and Afghanistan.
Ashokan inscriptions were generally placed on ancient highways.
Ashoka’s contemporaries were Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus, Magas and Alexander of Epirus.
The Ranyo Ashoka portrait-inscription was found at Kanganahalli.
The Kalinga War was fought in 261 BCE.
The Thirteenth Rock Edict records the Kalinga War.
The Kalinga Edict declares “all men are my children”.
After Kalinga, policy shifted from Bherighosha to Dhammaghosha.
Ashoka gave up physical occupation for cultural conquest.
Ashoka sent ambassadors of peace to Greece and West Asia.
Ashoka sent his son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitra to Ceylon.
Rock Edict 13 says 1,00,000 were killed and 1,50,000 deported in Kalinga.
Ashoka fought Kalinga in the eighth year of his reign.
Dhamma emphasised moral governance, social welfare and respect for all living beings.
Ashoka set the ideal of paternal kingship, treating subjects as his children.
Ashoka appointed Dhamma Mahamatras to spread Dhamma among all groups, including women.
Dhamma Mahamatras worked among various social groups including women.
Rajukas could both reward and punish people.
Ashoka’s teachings strengthened the family and the existing social order.
The Major Rock Edicts are a set of 14 inscriptions.
Rock Edict 1 prohibits animal sacrifice.
Rock Edict 4 records Bherighosha replaced by Dhammaghosha.
Rock Edict 2 provides medical care for men and animals and names the Cholas, Pandyas, Satiyaputras and Keralaputras.
Rock Edict 12 urges tolerance: whoever praises his own sect injures his own sect.
Rock Edict 3 orders Yuktas, Rajukas and Pradeshikas to tour every five years.
Rock Edict 8 replaces pleasure hunts with Dhammayatras.
Rock Edict 7 asks for tolerance among all sects.
Rock Edict 6 says the king wants to be told of public affairs at all times.
Pillar Edict V lists animals not to be killed and records the release of 25 prisoners.
Pillar Edict VI deals with the Dhamma policy.
Pillar Edict 7, the longest, appears only on the Delhi-Topra pillar moved by Firoz Shah Tughlaq.
The Allahabad pillar carries the Queen’s Edict of Karuvaki and the Schism Edict.
The Rummindei inscription commemorates the Buddha’s birthplace at Lumbini.
At Lumbini Ashoka exempted the village from bali and reduced bhaga to one-eighth.
The Bhabru (Bairat) edict states Ashoka’s faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha.
The Sohgaura (Saugara) copper plate records famine relief in Magadha.
Brahmagiri carries Minor Rock Edicts I and II on local administration.
The Kandahar edict is bilingual, in Greek and Aramaic.
The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes.
The 24 spokes represent the twelve causal links taught by the Buddha.
Erragudi in Andhra Pradesh has a set of Ashoka’s Major Rock Edicts.
Rajula Mandagiri in Kurnool (Andhra Pradesh) has an Ashokan Minor Rock Edict.
A fragment of an Ashokan pillar inscription was found at Amaravati.
Dhauli and Jaugada in Odisha carry the Separate Kalinga Edicts.
Kalsi (Uttarakhand) and Girnar (Gujarat) have Major Rock Edicts.
James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837.
The languages of Ashoka’s edicts were Prakrit, Greek and Aramaic.
In most of the subcontinent the edicts are in Prakrit written in Brahmi.
In the north-west the edicts use the Kharoshthi script.
In Afghanistan the edicts are in Aramaic and Greek.
Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra edicts are in Kharoshthi.
The Third Buddhist Council was held at Pataliputra under Ashoka.
The Third Buddhist Council met in 250 BC.
Moggaliputta Tissa presided over the Third Buddhist Council.
The Third Council aimed to purify the Sangha of corruption.
After the Third Council, missionaries went to Sri Lanka, Burma and other countries.
Ashoka is called the First Global Ambassador of India.
The king was assisted by a council whose advice was not binding.
High officers were chosen from among the councillors.
The chief functionaries (tirthas) included Mantrin, Purohita, Senapati and Yuvaraja.
The Yuvaraja was the crown prince.
The Arthashastra lists 18 tirthas, paid from 48,000 to 60 panas.
The Samaharta was the collector-general of revenue.
The Sannidhata was the chief treasury officer.
The Vyavaharika was chief justice of the civil court.
The Pradeshta was chief justice of the criminal court.
Dharmasthiya courts were civil and Kantakashodhana courts criminal.
Mauryan administration was backed by an elaborate system of espionage.
Spies were called Gudhapurushas, stationary (samstha) or wandering (sanchara).
There was an enormous gap between the highest and lowest servants.
The army had infantry, cavalry, elephants, chariots, navy and transport.
Sitadhyaksha ran crown farms, Panyadhyaksha commerce and Lakshanadhyaksha the mint.
The Antapala guarded frontier forts and the Nagaraka ran the city.
Provinces were placed under princes (Kumaras) as viceroys.
Taxila was the capital of Uttarapatha.
Suvarnagiri was the capital of Dakshinapatha.
Ujjain was the capital of Avantiratha.
Tosali was the capital of the eastern province (Kalinga).
The source text says provinces were governed by officials called Uparikas.
The Pradesika was the equivalent of a district magistrate.
Rajukas were like Patwaris, responsible for land survey and assessment.
The Yukta was a subordinate revenue officer at district level.
Sthanikas were collecting officers under the Pradesika.
The Gopa was responsible for accounts.
Rashtrapala/Kumara were viceroys in charge of provinces.
Pataliputra was run by six committees of five members each.
Separate arrangements existed for rural and urban administration.
Ashoka introduced rotation of officers at Ujjain, Taxila and Tosali.
Twenty-seven superintendents (adhyakshas) regulated economic activity.
Land tax varied from one-fourth to one-sixth of the produce.
The state held monopolies in mining, sale of liquor and manufacture of arms.
Punch-marked silver coins with peacock and hill-crescent symbols were the imperial currency.
The Mauryan state controlled all economic activities.
The state brought new lands under cultivation and demanded more crops in an emergency.
Taxes were also collected in kind, and assessment mattered more than storage.
Mauryan taxes included bhaga, bali and pindakara; Sita was state-owned land.
The Mauryans introduced stone masonry on a wide scale.
Mauryan artisans attained high skill in polishing stone.
Each pillar is a single piece of buff-coloured sandstone.
The Lion Capital of Ashoka from Sarnath is India’s national emblem.
The Barabar caves near Gaya are the earliest rock-cut caves.
The Lomas Rishi cave is in the Barabar hills.
An Ashokan pillar stands at Lauriya Nandangarh (Bihar).
The Bull capital comes from Rampurva.
Kumhrar (Patna) has the remains of an 80-pillared hall.
The Didarganj Yakshi was found near Patna.
The Sarnath capital’s abacus shows an elephant, horse, bull and lion.
India adopted the Lion Capital as State Emblem on 26 January 1950 with Satyameva Jayate.
The Barabar caves were given to the Ajivikas.
Mauryan conquest spread material culture through trade and missionary activity.
Northern Black Polished Ware was a hallmark of Mauryan material culture.
Burnt bricks were used for the first time in north-eastern India in this period.
Ring wells first appeared in the Gangetic plains during the Mauryan period.
Socketed axes, sickles and ploughshares appear, and the spoked wheel came into use.
Ashoka died in 232 BCE, after which the empire declined under weak successors.
The last Mauryan, Brihadratha, was assassinated by his general Pushyamitra Shunga.
Ashoka’s successors were Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan and Brihadratha.
Dasharatha gave the Nagarjuni caves to the Ajivikas.
Ashoka’s anti-sacrifice attitude caused a Brahmanical reaction.
Huge army and bureaucracy costs and grants to monks caused a financial crisis; gold images were melted.
Oppressive rule in the outlying provinces weakened the empire.
Spread of material knowledge let new kingdoms such as the Shungas, Kanvas and Chetis rise.
Neglect of the north-west frontier is a cause of the decline.
Unlike China’s Great Wall, Ashoka built no defence against nomads in the north-west.
Chandragupta became a Jain under Bhadrabahu and died at Shravanabelagola.
Chandragupta died by sallekhana, the Jain fast unto death.
Chandragupta’s governor Pushyagupta built the Sudarshana lake.
Ashoka’s governor Tushaspha added channels to the Sudarshana lake.
